Initial conditions

Boundary conditions

Within the finite-horizon equilibrium result, inherited expertise and frontier productivity are joined to the terminal value of qualification.

At the beginning of a filing season, the people available to advise households carry the learning acquired during earlier seasons, while a novice’s decision to study depends on the professional work expected ahead. In the shared research economy, inherited expertise EEE and frontier productivity AAA supply the initial states, while a terminal career payoff Δ‾\overline\DeltaΔ records the value of qualification in the continuation occupation.

Given a trial qualification-value path, we integrate population and frontier forward while clearing the labor market at each date. Using the resulting wages, we then integrate the value equation backward from its terminal payoff. Repeating these updates seeks agreement between physical evolution and anticipated earnings, following the construction in the paper’s finite-horizon existence proof.

Choosing a current qualification value changes study immediately and thus changes the population that later wages must clear, while those wages determine whether the original value was justified. Specifying the terminal payoff closes this relationship through what a qualification is worth after the modeled interval, allowing the initial value to adjust until the whole earnings path supports it.

Within a compact feasible region, uniformly decreasing service demand gives regular wage roots, bounded wages keep private values bounded, and a sufficiently short horizon limits the feedback between the two path updates. Proposition H.1 supplies an explicit contraction condition under which the boundary problem has one equilibrium inside that region, including endogenous changes in the active research allocation.

Research feedback

Conditional response

At a fixed frontier, the shared-wage derivative follows expert supply and service demand through research costs.

Through the shared market, more expertise lowers the human research wage, while greater customer demand raises it, and both price effects change the packets purchased by a fixed fund. At a common frontier in a strict human regime, Proposition G.2 differentiates clearing to give the displayed relationship, where dDS∣wdD_S|_wdDS​∣w​ includes customer and qualification-value effects evaluated at the original wage.

Preparing the figure

Customer preparation changes remaining work, received practice enters career accumulation, and the shared wage carries expertise into research costs, giving each part of the mechanism its own conditional relationship (fig. 10). For positive quantities uuu and vvv, the elasticity (u/v) ∂v/∂u(u/v)\,\partial v/\partial u(u/v)∂v/∂u expresses a local percentage response, while a derivative of an accumulation or value equation describes its corresponding flow.

When a customer or research change persists across time, the career equations and market clearing carry it into future practice, study, and available expertise, which in turn enter the frontier path. Joining those relationships closes the connection from customer work to the technology available to future customers (fig. 14), with complete paths selected by inherited states and the terminal career payoff.

Recursive improvement enters research through complete-method productivity, while the expert population enters through the labor required by the selected method. At a fixed frontier, human research has FE/F=1/(hJ)>0F_E/F=1/(h\mathcal J)>0FE​/F=1/(hJ)>0, so the expertise formed through customer work changes the research purchased by the fund. Within an interior mixed or autonomous allocation, FE=0F_E=0FE​=0, while the recursion continues through machine costs as the frontier advances.

When a machine route retains a human grounding requirement, expertise again increases research output at the grounded corner through the price of that required labor. Equal-cost mixing can still absorb population changes through method shares, so the customer-to-expertise channel and the frontier-to-research channel combine according to the complete allocation rule.

Career expectations

For a novice deciding whether this year’s tuition is justified by later professional work, comparing two future wage paths requires carrying their earnings differences back to the date of study. Subtracting the private value equations gives a scalar linear equation because the difference of squared values factors into their sum times their difference, and backward integration produces the positive kernel above.

With common terminal values, every future wage difference enters present qualification value with positive weight, so a lower future wage path lowers today’s study incentive. For bounded global value paths, the terminal term vanishes as the horizon grows, and the same comparison becomes an integral over the entire future, as proved in Proposition G.3.

Along a selected baseline, the local weight on a small wage increment during a future interval decays with ρ+δ+x(s)\rho+\delta+x(s)ρ+δ+x(s), combining ordinary discounting, obsolescence, and the novice’s own future opportunities to qualify (fig. 12). Faster future study narrows the extra advantage of already possessing qualification, while a wage change occurring after the valuation date still contributes positively whenever its interval lies inside the remaining career.

With an imposed wage increment, these weights carry a supplied earnings change through the private value equation, giving its conditional contribution to current study. When customer technology or research methods change, their wage path instead comes from the shared markets, so integrating the same positive weights follows the earnings consequences of the complete adjustment.

For an announced machine improvement, the wage difference comes from the endogenous research allocation and its frontier path, with the mixed-regime theorem giving a signed joint example under the relative-productivity condition. Through the kernel, future wage changes that differ in sign contribute according to their place along the full discounted path when determining current investment.

Selecting a path

At a fixed frontier, the stationary career system has one stable direction and one unstable direction under the strict diagnostic-portfolio conditions, so a nearby inherited expert population selects one locally convergent initial qualification value. Numerical selection can use forward and backward relaxation or vary the initial value until the terminal payoff is satisfied, with feasibility, clearing, and boundary residuals evaluated on the resulting path.

For a longer finite horizon, the shooting residual S(Δ0)=Δ(T)−Ψ(E(T),A(T))S(\Delta_0)=\Delta(T)-\Psi(E(T),A(T))S(Δ0​)=Δ(T)−Ψ(E(T),A(T)) gives a local selection test, since a nonzero derivative S′(Δ0)S'(\Delta_0)S′(Δ0​) allows the implicit-function theorem to identify one nearby initial value. Endogenous equal-cost boundaries preserve the wage level and use piecewise derivatives, while a discrete first-availability event also changes its date under perturbation.

Beginning from common population and frontier states, a change in practice, service demand, or machine requirements can move current prices and values before its accumulated effects appear in expertise and productivity (fig. 11). Comparing each path with the economy where both research methods are available follows that timing in proportional changes, while the qualification paths meet at their common terminal zero and proportional value differences are defined at earlier dates with positive baseline value.

At each date on the resulting path, work reaches people whose expertise was accumulated earlier, while their investment reflects the earnings expected from later work. Research uses current AI to produce a new frontier that returns both to subsequent research and to customer preparation, so frontier growth follows this recursion through complete-method productivity, available expertise, and the time needed to use an advance.
